catalog_quote: p.43 §3.2: "A disyllabic word is a word with two syllables. The strong stress always occurs on the last syllable of any disyllabic word and also the unstress or the weak stress occurs on another syllable of the word." p.45 §3.3: "A trisyllabic word is a word with three syllables. The strong stress always occurs on the last syllable of any trisyllabic word and also the unstress or the weak stress occurs on the non final syllable of the word." p.46 §4: "The phonological word structure are always predictable from the position in a word and from the syllabic structure of the word. Strong stress, which functions as the nucleus syllable of the word, always occurs on a monosyllabic word and on the final syllable of any polysyllabic word. Weak stress and unstress, which function as peripheral syllables occur preceding the final syllable of the word." [new paragraph] "The phonological word structures are predictable according to the rule stated above, therefore, it is non-phonemic then it is not necessary to write any stress mark on words in phonemic writing. And the word-boundaries are marked by / /."

new_statements.rule_in_words: The phonological word (one to three syllables) has exactly one strong-stressed syllable, always the final one (a monosyllable is itself strong-stressed); preceding syllables are weak-stressed or unstressed. Stress is predictable and non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A three-way phonetic scale: strong ('), weak (ˇ), unstressed. Non-final syllables carry weak stress or none: disyllables [S.'S] (e.g. m̩.'tu: 'door') or [ˇS.'S] (ˇdɔ:k.'maj 'flower'); trisyllables [S.ˇS.'S] or [ˇS.ˇS.'S] (ˇpa.ˇwi.'ni: 'custom'). p.42: among strong-stressed syllables, checked syllables and long-vowel syllables are phonetically stronger than smooth/short-vowel ones.
new_statements.exceptions: The reduced prefix m̩ (from the negative / fruit marker) and structural words (naŋ 'with', cak 'will') never take strong stress (p.41 fn.); syllabic m̩ cannot bear strong or weak stress (p.40); four ˇS.'S words (e.g. pʰa.'jɔ: > 'pʰjɔ:) collapse to monosyllables in fast speech (p.44); long vowels in non-final syllables are shortened (p.45).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' = stress group of 1-3 syllables in the author's tagmemic hierarchy; p.40 states this rank 'does not cover any compound words'. Tone is independent (six tonemes on every syllable). Data are citation/elicited forms from one main informant of Lue (Moeng Wa) at Baan Sanmafan, Amphoe Mae Suai, Chiang Rai.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Lue (self-designation 'Lue Moeng Wa') spoken at Baan Sanmafan, Tambon Tha Ko, Amphoe Mae Suai, Chiang Rai Province, Thailand — a diaspora Tai Lue community (migrants from Sipsongpanna), not the Jinghong/Chiang Rung standard described by Li 2022 and Hartmann 1984. Glottolog has no sub-dialect codes under luuu1242, so it maps to luuu1242 itself. Supporting (non-rule) remarks in Hartmann 1979/1984 concern Chieng Rung (Jinghong) Lue and Phillips & Hanna 2019 concern Xishuangbanna Lue; all are consistent with weak non-final / strong final syllables.

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine (1906). L’état actuel des études de linguistique générale: Leçon d’ouverture du cours de grammaire comparée au Collège de France, lue le mardi 13 février 1906. Revue des Idées: Études de Critique Générale 3. pp. 296-308.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 1257.10)
sources.note: Glottolog mis-attachment: 'lue' in the title is the French past participle of lire ('leçon.. lue le mardi 13 février 1906' = 'lecture.. read on Tuesday 13 February 1906'), not the language name Lue/Lü. The digital copy is the correct copy of the cited work, and the work treats general/Indo-European linguistics (French, Armenian, Indo-European examples), not Lue. The catalog record for Lue (Ploykaew 1985: strong stress on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words) is neither supported nor challenged by it.
